item.title: How Could Childhood Trauma Make You Sick?
item.description:
Trauma

How Could Childhood Trauma Make You Sick?

Chronic pain and illness may link back to a traumatic childhood.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • A growing body of evidence shows a link between childhood trauma and physical illness in adulthood.
  • Mind-body symptoms such as migraines, eczema, and digestive issues may stem from a traumatic childhood.
  • But these symptoms can be treated with skilled, holistic care—including trauma-informed therapy.
Source: Sasun Bughdaryan / Unsplash

How is your gut? I hope it’s gurgling away happily, digesting food, extracting nutrients, and dispatching waste as it was designed to do. But for many of us, including me, our gut is not a happy organ. I have long struggled with both acid reflux and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), neither of which is fun. It’s clear to me that these conditions, along with musculoskeletal problems and eczema, are stress-related—and that this stress is long-term, with roots in childhood trauma.

This is one of those connections—from early childhood to adulthood—that can be hard for folks to understand or even accept sometimes, so let’s explore it together. First, every physical illness clearly manifests in the body. I have a cold right now, and it is showing up, with annoying persistence, in my sinuses, nose, throat, and chest. And some illnesses, like my cold, are purely biological, caused by an invading pathogen. Others are purely the result of physical trauma, such as breaking your wrist when falling off a ladder.

But many illnesses involve mind-body symptoms, meaning they are a combination of the physical and psychological. All of the long-term conditions I struggle with fall into this category—the grey area where there isn’t an obvious physical or biological cause. Many autoimmune illnesses also fall into this category, such as multiple sclerosis (MS)1 and lupus,2 which both show links to trauma.

Evidence-based theory

There is now a wide range of evidence backing up the idea that stress in childhood—especially when it’s overwhelming or chronic—makes us vulnerable to developing both physical and mental health problems in later life.3 And stress is the key element of what makes traumatic incidents traumatic for us as children.

Let’s look at this through the lens of Mary’s story. Mary was raised in a highly dysfunctional family environment. Her mother was an alcoholic and, although her dad did his best to keep the family running, it was a struggle. "I remember so many times she forgot to collect me from school," says Mary. "Or was too drunk to drive, and I would have to walk home. From, like, 7 or 8 years old."

Mary also remembers all the shouting. "Mum was a mean drunk, so after a bottle of wine or two she would start screaming at me and my sister, telling us we were disgusting and ungrateful brats, stuff like that," says Mary sadly. "We were just scared all the time because you never knew when the bomb would go off."

For poor little Mary and her younger sister, childhood was intensely, relentlessly stressful. And this stress had a big impact on their little bodies. "I was always sick as a kid. One cold after another, I had all these digestive issues and kept throwing up when I ate. Plus migraines, rashes, being constipated all the time, weird aches and pains, you name it."

Overwhelmed by stress

As an adult, these childhood illnesses had morphed into some nasty autoimmune conditions, like rheumatoid arthritis in her hands and acid reflux so bad she needed major dental work to repair her teeth, which had been damaged by a lifetime’s acid erosion. In therapy, we spent a great deal of time with the terrified young parts of Mary, who felt like they were still stuck in that scary, noisy house with a drunken, volatile parent. Gradually, as we healed these little parts and Mary’s mind-body system settled, her physical complaints also eased.

Working in conjunction with a nutritionist and her medical team, we saw a great improvement in her physical symptoms, which was a huge relief to Mary. Her anxiety also eased off, and she felt strong enough to cut all contact with her mother, who continued to drink heavily and act abusively, well into her old age. Sometimes no contact is the only way when your family member refuses to change and keeps hurting you.

I hope you found this post informative and helpful in some way. And if you struggle with chronic pain or illness of any kind, I’m sorry. I know all too well how debilitating that can be. But please also know there is always hope if we take a holistic approach to any kind of ill-health, whether that’s mental or physical. Because you and I are a system—in fact, a system of systems—so trying to treat anything as if it’s a discrete, separate problem makes no sense.

We now have a wide range of evidence-based, trauma-informed therapy models that can help treat the root cause of mind-body symptoms, so if you are struggling, please do find a skilled, compassionate clinician to help with your healing. Working systemically, healing those psychological wounds in conjunction with medical help, focusing on your diet, sleep, exercise, alcohol and caffeine intake, nervous-system regulation, and a host of other helpful strategies could be life-changing.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What to Do After an Angry Outburst
item.description:
Anger

What to Do After an Angry Outburst

How mindfulness can help us recover from anger and return to balance.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Instead of pushing anger away, notice how it feels and moves through the body.
  • Naming anger more precisely can help us understand what we’re actually experiencing.
  • Self-compassion and forgiveness help interrupt shame and restore emotional balance.
Source: Unsplash/Simran Sood

Did you just blow your stack? That’s OK! Even the most calm, cool, and collected among us can lose their temper once in a while. You can’t avoid angry feelings all the time, and for those moments when you let anger get the best of you, there are ways you can cool down more quickly and minimize the damage, both to yourself and to others. Mindfulness is amazing for this—it can be deployed in any moment, offering a fresh start, a return to equanimity, and even creative solutions to problems that seemed impossible in the heat of the emotion.

It’s essential to remember, however, that the “miracle” of mindfulness comes from turning toward your experience, not away from it. And, because the experience of anger can be quite unpleasant, humor helps. If you’re a visual person, imagine donning your scuba gear and diving into the underwater world of the body, or opening the mouth of the fire-breathing dragon and putting your head inside. Or recite a silly mantra, like “c’mon anger, gimme all you got” or “I think I’ll just sit here for three minutes and self-combust.” Then try these steps. Here’s what to do after an angry outburst.

1. If possible, give yourself (and those around you) the gift of a time-out. It could be three minutes or 10, depending on how much time you have and need. This may involve going by yourself to another room, but it doesn’t have to.

2. Begin by tracking the physical “inner geography” of the emotion. Where in your body do you feel it? Explore the sensations of anger. You may be tempted to try to push them away. Instead, investigate how they feel in the body, noticing gross and subtle fluctuations throughout the field of physical sensation. Do they increase or decrease in intensity? Do they shift? If so, can you track their movement?

3. Now, see if you can silently name what you are experiencing. Start with the gross category of “anger,” and then see if you can refine your awareness enough to zero in on what flavor and intensity of anger you’re feeling. Is it irritation, frustration, annoyance, infuriation, rage, or even fury? Finding the right label is like hitting a tennis ball on the sweet spot of the racket—“ping!”

4. Try to bring compassion to the anger. This feeling is normal, part of being human; we all experience it at times. See if you can cradle your own anger like a mother cradling her newborn child. What happens as you hold it in this way, with tenderness and care?

5. Forgive yourself. The more readily you can forgive, the more quickly you can return to balance and take the next sane step. Remember—getting angry isn’t a crime! Criticizing yourself and keeping yourself on the hook will only entangle you in a cycle of shame and self-preoccupation. Self-forgiveness is the secret rocket booster to emotional balance.

A version of this article also appears in Mindful Magazine.

item.title: A Psychedelic Solution for Postpartum Depression?
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

A Psychedelic Solution for Postpartum Depression?

New research suggests promise of a short treatment for postpartum depression.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Treatments for postpartum depression are few but evolving.
  • Antidepressants can be effective, yet weeks are needed to reach recovery, and side effects may endure.
  • A new short-acting treatment, mebufotenin, shows promise.
Source: globalmoments / Getty Images

Alongside recent news of tragic outcomes in untreated postpartum psychosis, postpartum depression (PPD) and anxiety are significantly more prevalent—affecting one in five new mothers—and in urgent need of treatments. Mebufotenin, a psychedelic with a long history, offered surprisingly positive results in a recent trial (Johnson et al., 2026). PPD and postpartum mood and anxiety disorders (PMADs, which encompass PPD) are difficult to treat, yet affect both parent and infant—and frequently an entire family.

Treating PMADs is challenging for several reasons. Treatments must be well-tolerated by mother and—if she’s breastfeeding—infant. To gain wide acceptance, treatments need low side-effect profiles and low burden of use. Mothers need to be able to swiftly get back to supporting themselves and their newborn, and anyone else they choose to care for.

Traditionally, antidepressants work for PMADs, but women often wait weeks to access a prescriber and prescription, and additional weeks before experiencing positive effects (sometimes accompanied by negative side effects). Meanwhile, everyone in a family may suffer. (It’s important to note that severe postpartum depression or anxiety may have negative effects on infants and children, but maternal treatment of PMADs offers robust downstream recovery from any effects to infants and children too.)

Newer treatments for PMADs have been problematic. Brexanolone involved 3-4 days of inpatient IV treatment, so a mother was away from her baby. (Brexanolone has subsequently been removed from the market.) Zuranolone, though orally administered for 14 days and easier to use, can impair alertness to the point that patients are not to drive, and users report other side effects as well.

Mebufotenin is novel. A synthetic derivative of 5-MeO-DMT, sometimes called “The God Molecule,” DMT, or “Toad” (because it can be derived from toad venom, or plants), this substance—natural or synthetic—works on serotonin receptors like many antidepressants and psychedelics, but in an unusual way.

The recent mebufotenin study offers strong takeaways, and here’s what’s noteworthy:

  • Mebufotenin was highly effective. Although the study was small and a Phase 2a study (meaning further large, more rigorous studies are needed before approval), all 10 women experienced an approximate 95 percent reduction in depression scores by two hours after taking mebufotenin. They maintained these low scores at final testing, on day 8. In previous studies, 5-MeO-DMT has been shown to help with anxiety, substance use, bipolar II, posttraumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and other psychological disorders as well.
  • Mebufotenin was well tolerated. The drug appears to be safe, with few adverse side effects reported. Headache was the most common side effect, and all side effects were mild or moderate. Further, the positive psychological effects of mebufotenin offered “peak experiences” in seven of ten participants. Prior 5-MeO-DMT study participants have described these psychedelic effects as “ineffable,” or difficult to describe, using terms like “unity,” belonging to something greater than oneself, a sense of “pure being or awareness,” deep intuitive knowledge, and feelings of tenderness, peace, awe, amazement, and more.
  • Mebufotenin was convenient and fast. In this “proof of concept” study determining the drug’s effectiveness, participants took mebufotenin via inhalation up to three times (depending on individual experience) and went home the same day. Besides improved psychological functioning and mood, mothers reported improved maternal functioning as well. And, though traces of mebufotenin were immediately present in breast milk, they rapidly disappeared within 10 hours.
Source: fertnig / Gettty Images Signature

As with all research, several limitations deserve mention. Sample size was typical for a phase 2a trial, but too small to draw definitive conclusions. No control group was used, so all participants knew they were taking active drug, which could bias results. Long-term assessments of mood and functioning past day 8 are necessary. Some study researchers were paid by the company manufacturing synthetic mebufotenin, which can also bias results. Finally, the majority of study participants were white, so future research with diverse populations is critical. Yet, 5-MeO-DMT has been reportedly used by indigenous cultures for centuries. So it’s hoped that larger, more inclusive studies will reinforce the safety and promise of this intriguing substance—for PMADs, and many other psychological disorders as well.

item.title: The Emotions You Didn't Know You Were Sharing
item.description:
Leadership

The Emotions You Didn't Know You Were Sharing

If there's one thing we humans are generous with, it's our emotions.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions are contagious; we transmit them to others, often without realizing it.
  • Leaders' and speakers' moods directly influence their teams or audiences, for better or worse.
  • Managing your emotions is essential—your state can either inspire or destabilize those around you.

If there's one thing we humans are generous with, it's our emotions. We share them constantly—in person, on stage, even online—whether we mean to or not. Emotions spread like infectious diseases, and for leaders talking to their teams, and speakers talking to a room, that's both very good news and very bad news.

The good news first. If I'm genuinely excited about a big win or a new initiative, I can infect my team with that excitement just by talking to them about it. Speakers can do this too: We pass along our energy, our compassion, our grief, our anger, our joy—whatever the moment calls for—simply by feeling it "out loud" in front of an audience. Exactly how you do it is a matter of style, but begin with simply and clearly feeling it at the core of your being.

Now the bad news. If you're not aware of your own emotional state—and not able to manage it—you may end up sharing the wrong thing entirely. A nervous speaker who lets that nervousness show is dumping it straight on the audience, and nervous audiences don't listen as well as relaxed ones. They will close up instead of opening up. A leader who lets her rising panic about the company show is handing that panic to the whole team, right when she needs them focused, not spiraling.

Why Managing Emotions Is Essential for Leaders and Speakers

This is why managing your emotions isn't just optional for leaders and speakers—it's the whole ball of wax. I know that sounds counterintuitive. Emotions just happen to us, right? How do you manage something involuntary? But you actually can learn to set emotional intent, the same way you'd set any other intent. 5-4-3-2-1, as Mel Robbins says. Leaders do it in high-stakes negotiations all the time—staying calm on purpose because it leads to better outcomes, or even losing their temper strategically, at exactly the right moment, to signal what really matters to them. Speakers do it when walking out on stage, keeping their nerves in check because looking terrified in front of a crowd is rarely worth doing. Audiences (unfairly!) interpret nervousness as a lack of confidence in what you are saying.

And the research backs up just how contagious emotion really is. Stress spreads between people (Li et al., 2023), and so do emotions online. A Facebook study of over a billion posts across two years found positive emotions in particular spread through our networks (Coviello et al., 2014). Rudeness is contagious in the workplace (Foulk et al., 2015), but so are kindness (Jung et al., 2020) and empathy (Zhou et al., 2024). Even risky behavior spreads, as we model what the people around us are doing (Suzuki et al., 2016).

Everyday Contagious Behaviors

It’s not just the big stuff, either. Yawning is contagious (Norscia et al., 2011), and so is shivering (Harrison et al, 2014)—researchers have even used yawning as an informal test for psychopathy, since psychopaths are less likely to “catch” a yawn thanks to lower empathy (Rundle et al., 2015). Smiling spreads too (Hess & Bourgeois, 1991), and, amusingly, so does mobile phone use (Maglieri et al., 2021).

So, while you are learning to get your emotions under new management, here's an experiment to try: Take a day off from your mobile phone and just smile at people. Smile at your team. Smile at people you pass on the street. Smile at your barista. The results may surprise you!

item.title: Being at the Top Is Not the Same as Being Better
item.description:
Social Life

Being at the Top Is Not the Same as Being Better

Science gives no reason to confuse status, power, or wealth with human worth.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Social rank and status by themselves do not provide objective measures of an individual's worth.
  • Research does not show that having less status, power, or money has any objective meaning.
  • People at different levels of a social hierarchy have different responsibilities, not better or worse ones.

We live in a world that places enormous emphasis on being at the top. We are encouraged to make more money, gain more power, move higher within organizations, and achieve greater recognition. There is nothing inherently wrong with wanting any of these things. The problem comes when we assume that having them makes someone more important, more successful as a human being, or somehow better than people who have less.

From a scientific perspective, there is surprisingly little reason to make that assumption. Research on social hierarchies across animal species does not support the simple idea that individuals lower in a hierarchy necessarily experience greater stress, poorer health, or worse functioning than those at the top. Dominance can certainly provide advantages, including greater access to resources. However, the effects of rank vary considerably depending on the species and social environment, and being at the top can carry significant physiological and behavioral costs.

Robert Sapolsky's (2004) research on primates is particularly interesting in this regard. His work demonstrates that there is no universal relationship between low social rank and elevated stress. Whether dominant or subordinate animals experience greater physiological stress depends on characteristics of the particular social system. Being lower in a hierarchy is not inherently harmful. What matters considerably more is what that position actually means within a particular social environment.

Motivations Behind Valuing Hierarchical Status in Humans

This raises an interesting question when we turn to human hierarchies. The people who benefit most from a hierarchy have a strong reason to convince everyone else that their position is especially important. Someone with considerable wealth has an obvious incentive to believe that wealth is an important measure of success. Someone with considerable organizational power may similarly be inclined to believe that possessing power demonstrates greater importance. But the fact that people are motivated to believe something does not make it objectively true.

We see this constantly in modern society. Wealth, job titles, organizational authority, celebrity, and social influence are regularly treated as if they provide information about a person's underlying worth. Yet having more money primarily tells us that someone controls more financial resources. Having a higher position in an organization tells us that the person has greater authority within that organization. Neither fact, by itself, demonstrates that the individual is more valuable as a human being.

Animal social organization provides a useful comparison. Being higher in a hierarchy can mean having different responsibilities, greater access to resources, and greater influence over what happens within the group. It can also mean greater competition, more challenges from others, and greater costs associated with maintaining one's position. Individuals lower in a hierarchy may perform different functions that are no less necessary to the functioning of the group. Hierarchical position describes a relationship among individuals. It does not provide an objective measure of the inherent value of those individuals.

Workplace Roles and the Myth of Innate Importance

Consider the workplace. A corporate owner or executive develops plans, makes decisions, and directs resources. Other employees carry out many of those plans and perform the work necessary for the organization to function. These are different roles involving different responsibilities and different levels of authority. It does not logically follow that the person making the plan is inherently more important than the people whose work makes the plan possible.

The same reasoning applies to money. Having more money gives someone greater access to resources and greater ability to influence certain situations. Those are real advantages, and there is little reason to pretend otherwise. But greater access to resources is not the same thing as greater human worth. We make an enormous conceptual leap when we move from "this person has more resources" to "this person is therefore better or more important."

There is another reason to question these messages. People occupying privileged positions may be especially motivated to preserve systems of thinking that make those positions appear important. If my status contributes substantially to how I define myself, I have a reason to emphasize the importance of status. Convincing other people that my position deserves admiration can also help reinforce my own belief in its importance.

This becomes particularly relevant when someone makes you feel inadequate because you earn less money, have a less impressive title, possess less authority, or occupy a lower position in an organization. You do not need to deny that hierarchies exist. You also do not need to pretend that money and power have no practical advantages. You simply need to avoid adding a conclusion that the facts do not justify: that someone possessing more of these things is therefore a better or more important person.

The Psychology of Elevating Oneself by Diminishing Others

People sometimes try to elevate themselves by lowering the perceived value of others. When that happens, their judgment should not automatically become your judgment of yourself. Their need to emphasize their status may tell you considerably more about how they understand their own position than it tells you about your worth.

The research on social hierarchy provides a useful reminder. There is nothing in nature requiring every individual to be at the top, and being at the top is not automatically the best position under every circumstance. Hierarchies organize relationships, responsibilities, resources, and influence. We are the ones who make the additional mistake of turning those differences into judgments about who matters more.
